assets.title: What is a Binary Operation and a Closed Subset?
assets.body: A binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is a function mapping \(S \times S\) into \(S\), where \(*((a, b))\) is written \(a * b\). A subset \(H \subseteq S\) is closed under \(*\) if \(a * b \in H\) for all \(a, b \in H\); restricting \(*\) to \(H\) gives the induced operation on \(H\).

assets.title: What are Commutative and Associative Operations?
assets.body: An operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is commutative if \(a * b = b * a\) for all \(a, b \in S\). An operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is associative if \((a * b) * c = a * (b * c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in S\).

assets.title: What are an Identity Element and an Inverse Element?
assets.body: Let \(S\) be a set with binary operation \(*\). An element \(e \in S\) is an identity element for \(*\) if \(a * e = e * a = a\) for all \(a \in S\). If \(S\) has an identity \(e\), the inverse of \(x \in S\) is an element \(x' \in S\) such that \(x * x' = x' * x = e\).

assets.title: What is an Operation Table of a Binary Structure?
assets.body: A binary algebraic structure \(\langle S, * \rangle\) is a set \(S\) with a binary operation \(*\). On a finite set \(S\), an operation table lists elements in the same order down the left and across the top, placing \(a * b\) in the row of \(a\) and column of \(b\).

assets.title: What are Everywhere-Defined and Well-Defined Operations?
assets.body: To define a binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\): (Condition 1) exactly one element must be assigned to each ordered pair \((a, b) \in S \times S\) (everywhere defined and well defined, with no ambiguity); (Condition 2) the element \(a * b\) must belong to \(S\) (\(S\) is closed under \(*\)).

assets.title: What is an Idempotent Element?
assets.body: Let \(*\) be a binary operation on a set \(S\). An element \(a \in S\) is an idempotent for \(*\) if \(a * a = a\). By Exercise 43 (Section 1), if \(*\) is associative and commutative, the set \(H = \{a \in S \mid a * a = a\}\) of idempotents is closed under \(*\).

assets.title: What are a Group and an Abelian Group?
assets.body: A group \(\langle G, * \rangle\) is a set \(G\), closed under a binary operation \(*\), satisfying three axioms: \(\mathscr{G}_1\) associativity \((a * b) * c = a * (b * c)\); \(\mathscr{G}_2\) an identity \(e \in G\) with \(e * x = x * e = x\); and \(\mathscr{G}_3\) an inverse \(a' \in G\) for each \(a \in G\) with \(a * a' = a' * a = e\). A group \(G\) is abelian if \(*\) is commutative.

assets.title: What is a Group Isomorphism?
assets.body: Let \(\langle G_1, *_1 \rangle\) and \(\langle G_2, *_2 \rangle\) be groups. A function \(f : G_1 \to G_2\) is a group isomorphism if: (1) \(f\) is one-to-one and maps onto \(G_2\), and (2) \(f(a *_1 b) = f(a) *_2 f(b)\) for all \(a, b \in G_1\) (the homomorphism property). We write \(G_1 \simeq G_2\).

assets.title: What is a subgroup?
assets.body: A subset H of a group G is a subgroup of G if H is closed under the operation of G and forms a group under the induced operation.

assets.title: What is a cyclic subgroup?
assets.body: The cyclic subgroup generated by a is ⟨a⟩ = {aⁿ | n ∈ ℤ}. If ⟨a⟩ = G, then a is a generator and G is a cyclic group.

assets.title: What is the greatest common divisor?
assets.body: The greatest common divisor gcd(r,s) is the positive generator of {nr + ms | n,m ∈ ℤ}, so gcd(r,s) = nr + ms for some integers n and m.

assets.title: What is a group homomorphism?
assets.body: A map φ: G → G' between groups is a homomorphism if it preserves products: φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for all a, b in G.

assets.title: What is the kernel of a homomorphism?
assets.body: The kernel of a homomorphism φ: G → G' is Ker(φ) = {x ∈ G | φ(x) = e'}, the set of all elements mapping to the identity of G'.

assets.title: What is the left regular representation?
assets.body: The left regular representation φ: G → S_G maps each x to the permutation λ_x where λ_x(g) = xg. It is an injective homomorphism.

assets.title: What is a transposition?
assets.body: A transposition is a cycle of length 2. It interchanges two distinct elements while leaving every other element fixed.

assets.title: What is the permutation group \(S_A\)?
assets.body: For any nonempty set \(A\), the collection \(S_A\) of all permutations of \(A\) is a group under permutation multiplication \((\sigma\mu)(a) = \sigma(\mu(a))\).

assets.title: What is the symmetric group \(S_n\)?
assets.body: Let \(A = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\). The group of all permutations of \(A\) is the symmetric group on \(n\) letters, denoted \(S_n\), and has \(n!\) elements.

assets.title: What is a \(k\)-cycle and a transposition?
assets.body: A \(k\)-cycle \((a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)\) maps each listed number to the next and \(a_k\) back to \(a_1\), fixing all unlisted numbers. A 2-cycle \((a_1, a_2)\) is called a transposition.

assets.title: What are disjoint cycles?
assets.body: Cycles are disjoint if no number appears in more than one cycle. Every permutation in \(S_n\) is a product of disjoint cycles, unique up to cycle order and cyclic shifts.

assets.title: What is the orbit of an element under a permutation?
assets.body: For \(\sigma \in S_A\) and \(a \in A\), the orbit of \(a\) is the set \(\{\sigma^k(a) \mid k \in \mathbb{Z}\}\). For \(\sigma \in S_n\), it consists of the elements in the cycle of \(\sigma\) containing \(a\).

assets.title: Invariance of Parity (Theorem 8.19)
assets.body: Theorem 8.19: No permutation in \(S_n\) can be expressed both as a product of an even number of transpositions and as a product of an odd number of transpositions.

assets.title: What are even and odd permutations?
assets.body: A permutation of a finite set is even or odd according to whether it can be expressed as a product of an even number of transpositions or an odd number of transpositions.

assets.title: Subgroup of Even Permutations and \(\operatorname{sgn}\) (Theorem 8.24)
assets.body: For \(n \ge 2\), the even permutations in \(S_n\) form a subgroup of order \(n!/2\). The map \(\operatorname{sgn}: S_n \to \{1, -1\}\) is a homomorphism with kernel \(A_n\) (Exercise 52: determinants).

assets.title: What is the equivalence relation \(\sim_L\) modulo \(H\)?
assets.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\). The relation \(a \sim_L b\) if and only if \(a^{-1}b \in H\) is an equivalence relation on \(G\) that partitions \(G\) into disjoint cells.

assets.title: What is a left coset \(aH\)?
assets.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\). The subset \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\) of \(G\) is the left coset of \(H\) containing \(a\) (written \(a + H\) in additive notation).

assets.title: What is a right coset \(Ha\)?
assets.body: The relation \(a \sim_R b\) if and only if \(ab^{-1} \in H\) is an equivalence relation on \(G\) whose equivalence classes are the right cosets \(Ha = \{ha \mid h \in H\}\) of \(H\).

assets.title: Cosets of the Kernel of a Homomorphism (Theorem 10.17)
assets.body: Theorem 10.17: Let \(\phi: G \to G'\) be a group homomorphism with kernel \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \phi^{-1}[\{e'\}]\). Then the left and right cosets of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) are identical, and \(a, b \in G\) lie in the same coset iff \(\phi(a) = \phi(b)\).

objects.text: Each coset of Ker(φ) maps to one element in G'

assets.title: Theorem 16.2 (First Isomorphism Theorem) & Lemma 16.3
assets.body: Theorem 16.2: If \(\phi : G \to G'\) has kernel \(K\), there is a unique isomorphism \(\mu : G/K \to \phi[G]\) with \(\phi(x) = \mu(\gamma_K(x))\). Lemma 16.3: \(L \mapsto \gamma[L]\) bijects normal subgroups.

assets.title: Product HN, Join H v N, and Lemma 16.4
assets.body: For \(H, N \le G\), let \(HN = \{hn \mid h \in H, n \in N\}\), and let the join \(H \vee N\) be the smallest subgroup containing \(HN\). Lemma 16.4: If \(N\) is normal in \(G\), \(H \vee N = HN = NH \le G\).

assets.title: Theorem 16.5 (Second Isomorphism Theorem)
assets.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) and let \(N\) be a normal subgroup of \(G\). Then \((HN)/N \simeq H/(H \cap N)\) via the homomorphism \(\phi : H \to (HN)/N\) defined by \(\phi(h) = hN\) with kernel \(H \cap N\).

assets.title: Theorem 16.8 (Third Isomorphism Theorem) & Figure 16.9
assets.body: Let \(H\) and \(K\) be normal subgroups of \(G\) with \(K \le H\). Then \(H/K\) is normal in \(G/K\), and \(G/H \simeq (G/K)/(H/K)\) via \(\phi(gK) = gH\) with \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = H/K\).

assets.title: Definition 22.1: Ring
assets.body: A ring \(\langle R, +, \cdot \rangle\) is a set \(R\) with addition \(+\) and multiplication \(\cdot\) such that \(\mathcal{R}_1\) \(\langle R, + \rangle\) is an abelian group, \(\mathcal{R}_2\) \(\cdot\) is associative, and \(\mathcal{R}_3\) left and right distributive laws hold.

assets.title: Theorem 22.8 & Exercise 30 (Section 22): Sign Rules in a Ring
assets.body: If \(R\) is a ring with additive identity \(0\), then for all \(a, b \in R\): (1) \(0a = a0 = 0\), (2) \(a(-b) = (-a)b = -(ab)\), and (3) \((-a)(-b) = ab\). Exercise 30 (Section 22): \(R\) need not have \(1\).

assets.title: Definition 22.9: Ring Homomorphism and Kernel
assets.body: For rings \(R\) and \(R'\), a map \(\phi : R \to R'\) is a homomorphism if \(\phi(a + b) = \phi(a) + \phi(b)\) and \(\phi(ab) = \phi(a)\phi(b)\) for all \(a, b \in R\). Its kernel is \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{a \in R \mid \phi(a) = 0'\}\).

assets.title: Definition 22.12: Ring Isomorphism & Exercise 38 (Section 22)
assets.body: An isomorphism \(\phi : R \to R'\) from a ring \(R\) to a ring \(R'\) is a ring homomorphism that is one-to-one and onto \(R'\). The rings \(R\) and \(R'\) are then isomorphic (an equivalence relation by Exercise 38 (Section 22)).

assets.title: Definition 22.14: Commutative Ring, Ring with Unity, and Zero Ring
assets.body: A ring in which multiplication is commutative is a commutative ring. A ring with a multiplicative identity \(1\) is a ring with unity; \(1\) is unique (Theorem 1.15) and called unity. In the zero ring \(\{0\}\), \(0\) is unity.

assets.title: Definition 22.16: Unit, Division Ring, and Field
assets.body: In a ring \(R\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\), an element \(u \in R\) is a unit if it has a multiplicative inverse in \(R\). If every nonzero element is a unit, \(R\) is a division ring (skew field). A field is a commutative division ring.

assets.title: Subrings, Subfields, and Exercises 34 & 50 (Section 22)
assets.body: A subring of a ring \(R\) (or subfield of a field \(F\)) is a subset that is a ring (or field) under induced operations (written \(K \le L\)). By Exercise 50 (Section 22), \(S \le R\) iff \(0 \in S\), \(a - b \in S\), and \(ab \in S\).

assets.title: Definition 23.2: Divisors of 0 (Zero Divisors)
assets.body: If \(a\) and \(b\) are two nonzero elements of a ring \(R\) such that \(ab = 0\), then \(a\) and \(b\) are divisors of 0 (or 0 divisors). In a ring with unity, no unit can ever be a divisor of 0.

assets.title: Theorem 23.3 & Corollary 23.5: Units and 0 Divisors in Z_n
assets.body: Theorem 23.3: For \(m \in \mathbb{Z}_n\), either \(m = 0\), \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) (so \(m\) is a unit in \(\mathbb{Z}_n\)), or \(\gcd(m, n) > 1\) (so \(m\) is a 0 divisor). Corollary 23.5: \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is a field for every prime \(p\).

assets.title: Theorem 23.6: Cancellation Laws and Divisors of 0
assets.body: The multiplicative cancellation laws hold in \(R\) if \(ab = ac\) or \(ba = ca\) with \(a \ne 0\) implies \(b = c\). Theorem 23.6: The cancellation laws hold in a ring \(R\) if and only if \(R\) has no divisors of 0.

assets.title: Definition 23.7: Integral Domain
assets.body: An integral domain \(D\) is a commutative ring with unity \(1 \ne 0\) that contains no divisors of 0. By Theorem 23.6, the multiplicative cancellation laws always hold in an integral domain.

assets.title: Figure 23.10: Hierarchy of Rings & Exercises 24, 26 (Section 23)
assets.body: Every field is an integral domain because every nonzero element is a unit (hence never a 0 divisor). Figure 23.10 shows 6 regions: (1) Fields \(\mathbb{Q}\), (2) Domains \(\mathbb{Z}\), (3) \(\mathbb{Z}_6\), (4) \(2\mathbb{Z}\), (5) \(M_2(\mathbb{R})\), (6) \(M_2(2\mathbb{Z})\).

assets.title: Theorem 23.11: Every Finite Integral Domain is a Field
assets.body: Theorem 23.11: Every finite integral domain is a field. The finiteness condition is necessary because \(\mathbb{Z}\) is an infinite integral domain that is not a field (\(f(x) = 2x\) on \(\mathbb{Z}\) is one-to-one but not onto).

assets.title: Definition 23.12 & Example 23.13: Characteristic of a Ring
assets.body: If a positive integer \(n\) exists such that \(n \cdot a = 0\) for all \(a \in R\), the least such positive integer is the characteristic of \(R\); if no such \(n\) exists, \(R\) has characteristic 0. Example 23.13: \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{Z}_n) = n\), \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{Z}) = 0\).
